clue.text: Arm of church body organised harvest festival time after time

indicators.note: after places what comes before it in the clue behind the final abbreviation

parts.note: ran means organised, as in ran the show
Sept, short for September, is when harvest festivals are held

explanation.surface: A church group organised its harvest festival, as it does time after time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'time after time' looks like a stock phrase meaning repeatedly, but the first 'time' belongs to the harvest piece and 'after' is the order signal; 'body' completes the definition, a church building.
explanation.definitionFit: A transept is either of the two side arms of a cross-shaped church building.

clue.text: Impact tails off but with impromptu afterword

indicators.note: the tails of the four following words are their final letters, taken in turn

explanation.surface: An impromptu postscript tacked onto a speech makes its impact fizzle out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tails off' looks like a phrase meaning dwindles, but it asks for the last letter of each of the next four words.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull heavy sound of a blow is an impact, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: In place of sermon, lad's confession is brief

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the final letter of the confession is dropped

parts.note: a lad admitting what he is might say '(I) am boy'

explanation.surface: In church, a boy's confession turns out to be short.
explanation.walkthrough: The lad owns up 'am boy', and 'is brief' docks its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambo is a raised pulpit or reading desk in early churches, the place from which a sermon is delivered.

clue.text: Black eye limiting naval officer with his employer?

indicators.note: limiting means enclosing, so the black eye wraps round the officer and the abbreviation

parts.note: a shiner is slang for a black eye
PO is a petty officer in the navy

explanation.surface: A naval officer has a black eye, perhaps courtesy of the man who employs him.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition only works with the naval officer in mind: whoever owns the ship employs its crew.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who owns a vessel employs the sailors and officers who serve aboard it.

clue.text: Passenger, perhaps, sinking fitting into narrow compartment

parts.note: the passenger pigeon is one kind of the bird, hence 'perhaps'
holing a putt in golf means sinking it

explanation.surface: A traveller is being squeezed into a cramped compartment on a train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passenger' suggests a traveller; it is the extinct passenger pigeon.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigeonholing is literally slotting something into a small cubbyhole in a desk or cabinet.

clue.text: Paces rapidly round stores a fair distance

indicators.note: round means turned about, so the run of letters is read backwards
stores means holds inside, so the two words contain the letters wanted

explanation.surface: Someone pacing quickly around a shop's stockrooms covers quite a distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paces rapidly' invites an anagram of PACES round R; instead 'stores' hides CESRAP across the two words and 'round' turns it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsec is an astronomical unit of about 3.26 light years, so a considerable distance by any measure.

clue.text: Sailor died clutching minute weapon

parts.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman

indicators.note: clutching means holding, so the abbreviation for died grips the small letter

parts.note: OB, short for Latin obiit, means died

explanation.surface: A sailor died holding a tiny weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minute' reads as tiny, but it is M for minute.
explanation.definitionFit: An atom bomb is a nuclear weapon of mass destruction.

clue.text: Feigned dislike, consequently encourages to accept blame

parts.note: so means consequently or therefore

indicators.note: to accept means to take in, so the encouraging word receives the blame inside

parts.note: urges means encourages or spurs on
rap means blame, as in taking the rap

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to take the blame and so feigns disinterest.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase from Aesop's fox describes pretending to despise something one cannot have.

clue.text: It's worthless to preserve dignity in extremes, following defeat

parts.note: to can food is to preserve it

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
a loss is a defeat

explanation.surface: Keeping one's dignity after a defeat is said to be pointless.
explanation.definitionFit: Spun sugar that melts to nothing is a byword for something insubstantial and of no worth.

clue.text: Town's university and two others combined to dismiss Head

indicators.note: dismissing the head means removing the first letter

parts.note: Oxford and Cambridge combined make the portmanteau Oxbridge

explanation.surface: A university town is merged with two others and its head is sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'Town's' stands for 'is' joining definition to wordplay. UXBRIDGE is a town in west London, home of Brunel University.
explanation.definitionFit: Uxbridge is a town on the western edge of Greater London, so a straightforward example of a town.

clue.text: Do without chimney in which smoke could rise

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the swindle surrounds the chimney

parts.note: to do someone is to con or swindle them
lum is a Scots and northern word for a chimney

explanation.surface: A house manages without a chimney, though smoke might still rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do without' reads as 'manage without', but 'without' means outside here.
explanation.definitionFit: Smoke rises in a column, a tall vertical shaft or pillar of it.

clue.text: Lob bottle out over sea, with flares

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the preceding letters sit above the next piece
out signals that the letters are thrown out of their order

parts.note: the Med is the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: Someone lobs a bottle out to sea, perhaps with distress flares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flares' looks like signals fired at sea; they are wide-legged trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Bell-bottomed trousers widen from the knee, which is exactly what flared trousers do.

clue.text: March in cold round isolated wet area in field

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
the round letter O
lone means isolated or solitary

indicators.note: in places the wet area inside the field word

parts.note: a ley is a field or meadow
a bog is marshy wet ground

explanation.surface: Marching in the cold round a lonely boggy patch of a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like a verb or the month; it is the famous military march by Kenneth Alford.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a well-known British military march, often whistled, written in 1914.

clue.text: Childishly pictured man as a sort of model

definitions.meaning: a figure drawn by a child with straight lines for limbs and body
a model built by gluing together many small wooden sticks

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from slender sticks: stick-figure drawings and models glued from spent ones.

clue.text: I look regal when touring Australian town

indicators.note: touring means travelling around, so these letters wander into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone claims to look regal while touring the outback.
explanation.definitionFit: Kalgoorlie is a gold-mining town in Western Australia, an example of an Australian town.

clue.text: Ace leading at full speed

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace in cards
main means leading or chief

explanation.surface: An ace racer leads, going flat out.
explanation.definitionFit: Amain is an old word meaning with full force or at top speed.

clue.text: Entirely sound, good bar that is object of quest

indicators.note: sound tells us to take the word as it is spoken, not as written

parts.note: wholly means entirely
a rail is a bar

explanation.surface: A completely sound, good bar is what someone is searching for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective meaning healthy; here it signals that WHOLLY is heard and spelt HOLY.
explanation.definitionFit: The cup of Christ was the object of the Arthurian knights' quest, and figuratively any long-sought goal.

clue.text: Economist to get by smoothly talking up Scottish football team

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to blag is to obtain something by persuasive talk
Raith Rovers is a football club from Kirkcaldy in Scotland

explanation.surface: An economist gets ahead by smooth talk about a Scottish football side.
explanation.walkthrough: J. K. Galbraith was the Canadian-American economist.
explanation.definitionFit: John Kenneth Galbraith was a renowned economist, author of The Affluent Society.

clue.text: A little smoke from one article in cooker — concern about this

indicators.note: concern placed about this means it surrounds all that has gone before

parts.note: Co is short for company, a concern or business
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: in places the article inside the cooker word

parts.note: a grill is part of a cooker
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone frets about a small cigar lit from the cooker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concern' looks like worry; it is a business, CO.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigarillo is a small thin cigar, so literally a little smoke.

clue.text: Deposit smaller amount, saving nothing

indicators.note: saving means keeping safe within, so the smaller amount holds the zero

parts.note: less means a smaller amount
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone deposits a smaller sum, saving nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deposit' suggests a bank; it is a geological deposit.
explanation.definitionFit: Loess is a fine wind-blown sediment, a geological deposit.

clue.text: Decline in inflation not noticed, but outcome is flat

definitions.text: Decline in inflation not noticed, but outcome is flat

parts.words: Decline in inflation not noticed, but outcome is flat
parts.note: reads like economics, but describes a tyre losing air gradually unnoticed until it goes flat

explanation.walkthrough: The economic picture of inflation and a flat outcome describes a tyre leaking air.
explanation.definitionFit: A gradual leak in a tyre lets the pressure fall unnoticed until the tyre is flat.

clue.text: A knight evidently snapped, displaying great fear

indicators.note: a photograph displaying something holds it within the frame

parts.note: a pic is a photo, something evidently snapped
N is the chess notation for knight

explanation.surface: A knight clearly snapped, showing terror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snapped' suggests breaking; it is a photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: Panic is sudden overwhelming fear.

clue.text: Old person in race oddly eclipsed bionic man

indicators.note: with the odd letters blotted out only the even-placed ones remain

explanation.surface: A runner in a race is beaten by a bionic man.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas were an ancient people of Peru, so one was a member of that old race.

clue.text: Place to eat a dog's breakfast

definitions.meaning: British slang for a muddle or shambles

explanation.definitionFit: A forces' dining room and a chaotic shambles share the one word.

clue.text: Such revenue once from the seaside

definitions.meaning: the UK tax authority was formerly called the ... Revenue
away from the coast, towards the interior

explanation.walkthrough: The Inland Revenue was the British tax office until 2005.
explanation.definitionFit: The word named the old British tax office and means located away from the coast.

clue.text: Be strangely taken with cinema's atmosphere

indicators.note: strangely means the letters behave oddly and fall into a new order

parts.note: the possessive adds no letter, giving just the word itself

explanation.surface: Being oddly captivated by a cinema's atmosphere.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambience is the mood or feeling of a place, its atmosphere.

clue.text: Chap traditionally hanging outside very small grouse

indicators.note: outside means the hangman's name goes round the single letter

parts.note: Jack Ketch was a notorious English executioner, his name later used for any hangman

explanation.surface: A chap is traditionally hung for a very minor gripe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grouse' looks like the game bird; it is a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: To kvetch, from Yiddish, is to complain or gripe, a small grouse.

clue.text: American set a dish on a bust

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone places a dish on a sculpted bust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' looks like a sculpture; it means broken.
explanation.definitionFit: Idahoans are people of the US state of Idaho, a set of Americans.
